The Constitutional Development 
of India
Acts Passed for the British East India
Company Rule (1773-1853)
The Regulating Act of 1773 designated the governor 
of Bengal, Warren Hastings, as the Governor General of Bengal 
and subsumed the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay under 
Bengal's control. *The Governor General was provided with 
an executive council of four to assist him in Military and Non 
- Military decisions which would be made by the majority of 
the council. *Governor General could vote only in case of tie, 
in other words Governal-General had a casting vote in case 
of an equal division. *A Supreme Court which had a Chief 
Justice and three other Judges, was established at Fort William 
in Calcutta in the year 1774 by this Act. This Act prohibited 
the Servants of the company from engaging in private trade 
or accepting gifts and bribes from the Indians. * The British 
Government strengthened its control over the company through 
the Court of Directors (Governing body of The Company) to 
report on its revenue, civil and military affairs in India.
*Pitts India Act 1784 distinguished between the commercial 
and political functions of the company. *Board of Control
was created for political matters, and the Court of Directors 
controlled the commercial affairs. *Board of Control was 
comprised of 6 people.
*Act of 1786 provided that Governor General could overrule 
his council in matters of importance affecting the safety, 
peace or interest of the Empire in India. *Governor General 
was granted the powers of Commander-in-Chief. *Lord 
Cornwallis was the first Governor General to enjoy these powers. 
*The Charter Act of 1793 further extended the commercial 
monopoly of the company for another 20 years. *Charter 
Act of 1813 for the first time, made provision of at least 1
nd Governance 
Lakh rupees per year to be spent on the education, revival 
and improvement of literature, etc. of Indians. It ended the 
company's monopoly over trade, although the monopoly over 
trade of tea & trade with China continued.
*Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor General of Bengal 
the Governor General of India and vested in him all civil and 
military powers. *Lord William Bentinck became the first 
Governor General of India. *It ended the Activities of East 
India Company as a commercial body, which became purely 
an administrative body. *A legal member (fourth member)
was included in the council (executive) of Governor General. 
*Macaulay was the first legal member. This law member was 
entitled to act only for legislative purposes.
*Charter Act of 1853 separated for the first time the legislative 
and executive functions of the Governor General's council. *It 
established a separate Indian (Central) legislative council for 
law-making. *It introduced an open competition system for the 
selection and recruitment of Civil Servants.

Constituent Assembly and making 
of the Constitution
*The first formal demand for the Constituent Assembly
was made by the Swaraj Party at a conference in Ranchi held 
in May, 1934. *The idea of a Constituent Assembly was put 
forward for the first time by M.N. Roy in the year 1934. *The 
Indian National Congress officially demanded (after the Swaraj 
Party) a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution of India 
for the first time in May 1934, at Patna. *In 1938, Jawahar Lal 
Nehru, on behalf of the INC, declared that the constitution of 
free India must be framed, without outside interference, by a 
constituent Assembly elected on the basis of adult Franchise. The 
Demand was finally accepted in principle in the August offer 
of 1940. *The Constituent Assembly was constituted under 
the scheme formulated by the Cabinet Mission Plan 1946. 
*Number of representatives from provinces was based on their 
population i.e. about One representative per 10 Lakh people.
Of these, 296 were to be allotted to British India and 93 Seats to 
the Princely States. Out of 296 seats allotted to British India, 292 
members were to be drawn from the eleven governor's provinces 
and four from the four Chief Commissioners' provinces, one 
from each. *The representatives of Princely states were to be 
nominated by the heads of the Princely states. *The elections to 
the constituent assembly for 296 seats were held in July-August 
1946. The Indian National Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim 
League won 73 seats, and the small groups and independents 
got the remaining 15 seats. *In the beginning, Princely states 
did not participate in the Constituent Assembly, but with the 
third session of the Constituent Assembly commencing on 28 
April, 1947 the representatives of the Princely States of India 
began to join it gradually. *Constituent Assembly was a result 
of an Indirect election. *This election was not based on the 
Adult franchise. *According to Government of India Act 
1935, voting rights were limited and based on tax, education 
and property. *The Viceroy invited the elected representatives 
for the first meeting of Constituent Assembly on 9 December 
1946. *207 members participated in the first meeting. The 
meeting was presided over by Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha, 
the temporary President. Later, on 11 December 1946, Dr. 
Rajendra Prasad was unanimously elected as the President of 
the Constituent Assembly. It took 2 years, 11 months and 17 
days (according to the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha website) 
to complete the task of Constitution making. *A Total of 11 
Sessions (165 days) were held. *On 26 November 1949, i.e. the 
last day of 11th session, the Constitution was adopted. Except 
for these 11 sessions the constituent assembly finally met 
on 24 January 1950 to get the signatures of the members 
on the constitution. *Benegal Narsing Rau (B.N. Rau) was 
appointed as the constitutional advisor to the assembly. *On 26 
November 1949, the people of India adopted, enacted and gave
to themselves the constitution of India .*Some provisions of the 
constitution came into force on 26 November 1949 itself but it 
completely came into force on 26 January 1950. *The number 
of women in the constituent assembly was 15. *They were 1- 
Vijayalakshmi Pandit, 2- Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, 3- Sarojini 
Naidu, 4- Sucheta Kripalani, 5- Purnima Bannerjee, 6- Leela 
Roy, 7- G . Durgabai, 8- Hansa Mehta, 9- Kamala Choudhry, 
10- Renuka Ray, 11- Malati Choudhury, 12- Dakshayani 
Velayudhan, 13- Begum Aizaz Rasul, 14- Annie Mascarene 
and 15- Ammu Swaminathan. 
*The Interim government of India was formed on 2 
September, 1946; however, it did not include any member from 
the Muslim League. *Finally on 26 October 1946, 5 Members 
of the Muslim League were also included in the Cabinet.

Sources of the Constitution
*A major portion of the Indian Constitution is borrowed 
from the Government of India Act 1935 (Blue Print of 
Indian Constitution). *Rule of law, Parliamentary form of 
government, Cabinet System, Single Citizenship, Bicameral 
Legislature, Law making procedures, Parliamentary Privileges 
and prerogative writs are provisions borrowed from the 
Constitution of Britain. *Preamble, Judicial review, 
Independence of Judiciary, Fundamental rights, the post of 
Vice-President, the procedure of impeachment of President and 
removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges are provisions 
taken from the Constitution of the USA. *DPSP (Directive 
Principle of State Policy), method of election of President 
and nomination of members to the Council of States (Rajya 
Sabha) are provisions inspired by the Constitution of Ireland. 
*Federation with a strong centre, Advisory jurisdiction of the 
Supreme Court, residuary powers to be vested in the centre 
and appointment of Governors by the centre are provisions 
borrowed from Constitution of Canada. 
*Joint sitting of both houses of the Parliament, language of 
Preamble, Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and 
idea of concurrent list are borrowed from Constitution of 
Australia. *Provision related to Emergency (except Financial 
emergency) imported from Constitution of Germany. 
Procedure Established by law from Japan, procedure of the 
Constitutional Amendment and election of members of Rajya 
Sabha are borrowed from South Africa. *Fundamental Duties 
and the ideals of Justice (social, economic and political) in the 
preamble are imported from the USSR. The Republican system, 
principle of liberty, equality and fraternity in the preamble are 
borrowed from the Constitution of France.

The Preamble *The Objectives Resolution was moved to the Constituent 
Assembly on 13th December 1946 by Pt. Jawahar Lal Nehru, and 
it was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947. 
Later, this Resolution became the foundation of the Preamble. 
*The words ‘Socialist’, ‘Secular’, and ‘Integrity’ were 
incorporated in the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional 
Amendment Act 1976.

*The Preamble declares India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, 
Democratic Republic. It secures for all its citizens, justice of 
three types – social, economic and political. It is very helpful 
in the legal interpretation of the Indian Constitution. *In the 
words of Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, “The Preamble to our 
Constitution expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long”. 
*The Supreme Court accepted it as a part of the Constitution 
in the Keshavanand Bharti case(1973). *Before this, in the 
Berubari case (1960), the Preamble was not considered a 
part of the Constitution. *In Golaknath vs State of Punjab 
(1967), the preamble was considered as the core soul of the 
Constitution. *In Bommai vs Union of India (1994), the 
Supreme Court again gave the concept that the Preamble is a 
part of the Constitution. 
*It is non – justiciable in nature. *It talks about the freedom of 
faith, belief, worship, expression and thought. *It also ensures 
dignity and equal status and opportunities for all. *It is called 
the soul of the Constitution. 
*Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called the right to Constitutional 
remedies (Art. 32) as the heart and soul of the Constitution. 
*K. M. Munshi called the Preamble the political horoscope. 
*Subhash Kashyap said that, if the Constitution is the body then 
the preamble is the soul; if the Constitution is the building then 
the preamble is the foundation stone. 
*Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said that “the Constitution is a pious 
paper.”

The Governance System
*A Government is an institution or a system made of a group of 
people that takes care of or manages a country or a State. Every 
Government has its own Constitution or a set of fundamental 
principles that it follows to ensure effective governance. *An 
autocracy is a form of Government where the supreme power 
or rule is in the hands of one individual or entity. *Autocracy 
includes an absolute monarchy, where a family or a group of 
families rule a country. *The post of monarch is inherited in 
an absolute monarchy. *Monarchy is one of the oldest forms 
of Government. Now, autocracy also includes dictatorship. 
*Dictatorship is a form of Government in which an individual 
possesses absolute power without any effective limitations. 
*Democracy is the most widely adopted system of Governance 
h on TG-@freepdfhall

[[PDF_PAGE:71]]
at present. In this form of Government, the final power resides 
with the people. *The State has four essential elements - 
Population, Territory, Government and Sovereignty. 
Sovereignty is the most important element. *India, before 1947, 
was not a State because though it had three other elements, 
i.e. population, territory and Government; the fourth and most 
important one, i.e. sovereignty, was missing because of British 
control over India. * There are mainly two types of systems of 
Governance – Parliamentary and Presidential. *India follows 
a Parliamentary form of government which is influenced by 
the Parliamentary system of the United Kingdom. *In the 
Parliamentary system, members of the executive branch are 
usually taken from the Legislature and are also accountable to 
the legislature. The Parliamentary system of Government is also 
known as the Cabinet form of Government. *The government is 
responsible to the popular House of the legislature and remains 
in power till it has the support of a majority of members in that 
House. Thus, the Cabinet form of Government is a mechanism to 
ensure the collective responsibility of the Government to House 
of the people. *In India, the Cabinet is headed by the Head of the 
Government, the Prime Minister. *The Head of the State is the 
President. *India is a Democratic Republic where the Supreme 
power is vested in the people of India. *The Indian political 
system does not provide for a unified authority but makes a 
division of powers between the Union and the States. *The 
Indian Constitution has both Federal and Unitary features. In 
its Federal characteristic, it has a written Constitution, division 
of powers between centre and States, independent judiciary and 
bicameral legislature, etc. *However, it also includes unitary 
features like single citizenship, the appointment of Governors 
by the President, Declaration of emergency and the power of 
parliament for implementation of international agreements. *In 
the Presidential form of Government, the President is the head 
of the executive branch. *The best example of the Presidential 
form of Government is the Government of the USA. Granville 
Austin described Indian Federalism as Cooperative Federalism. 
K.C. Wheare describes it as Quasi – federal. Dr. B.R. 
Ambedkar stated that the Constitution has not been set in a 
tight mould of federalism, that is, it contains both federal and 
unitary features.

National Symbols
*The National Flag (Tricolour) is rectangular in shape and 
consists of three colours. *The ratio of the length of the flag to 
its width is 3:2. *The colour of the top band is Indian saffron 
(Kesariya) (symbol of strength and courage), the middle 
band is white (symbol of peace and truth) and the bottom is 
Indian green (symbol of fertility, growth and auspiciousness 
of the land). *In the centre of the white band is a navy blue 
wheel, which represents the Ashoka chakra. It has 24 spokes, 
and its design is that of the wheel, which appears on the abacus 
of the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka. *It is the symbol of 
Justice- (Wheel of the law/Dharma Chakra). *The National 
flag was designed by Pingali Venkayya. *The present design 
of the national flag was adopted by the constituent assembly 
on 22 July, 1947. *The description of the importance of three 
colours and a wheel (chakra) in our national flag by Dr. S. 
Radhakrishnan is mentioned and reproduced in the Flag code 
of India.
*The state emblem is an adaptation of the Sarnath lion 
capital of Ashoka. *It was adopted by the Government of 
India on 26 January, 1950. *The words 'Satyameva Jayate'
from Mundaka Upanishad are inscribed at the bottom in the 
Devanagari Script. *The National Anthem of India 'Jana Gana 
Mana.....' was officially adopted by the constituent assembly 
on 24th January, 1950. *It was first sung on 27th December, 
1911 at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress 
(President- Pt. Bishan Narayan Dar). *It was authored by 
Rabindra Nath Tagore. The Playing time of the full version is 
approximately 52 seconds. *The song 'Vande Mataram' was 
adopted as the national song by the constituent assembly on 
24 January, 1950. It is taken from the novel "Anand Math" 
authored by Bankimchandra Chatterjee. *It was first sung at 
the 1896 session of the Indian National Congress (President 
-Rahimatullah Sayani).
*The National Calendar based on the Saka era (Chaitra as its 
first month and Falgun as the last) was adopted on 22nd March, 
1957 along with the Gregorian Calendar. Generally, the month 
of Chaitra begins on 22 March, but in the leap years, it begins 
on 21 March.
*The National Flower of India is the Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera 
Gaertn). The National fruit is Mango (Magnifera Indica). 
*The National tree is the Banyan tree (Ficus benghalensis).
*While the government has clearly stated in the Rajya Sabha 
that no notification has been issued regarding India having a 
National flower. *The National Animal is the magnificent Tiger 
(Panthera tigris). *The National Bird is the Indian Peacock
(Pavo cristatus). *The National Aquatic animal is the mammal 
Ganges River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica).
*The river Ganga was declared the national river by the 
government of India in the year 2008. *The Government of 
India declared the Independence Day (15 August), Republic 
Day (26 January) and the Birth Anniversary of Mahatama 
Gandhi (2 October) as National Days.

States and the Union Territories
*The Indian Independence Act of 1947 led to the formation of 
two independent and separate Dominions – India and Pakistan. 
The Princely States were provided three options – to join India, 
to join Pakistan or to remain Independent. *There were more 
than 560 princely States within the Indian territory, out of which 
most joined India, whereas three (Hyderabad, Junagadh and 
Kashmir) refused to join India. *Later on, Hyderabad through 
military Action, Junagadh through a referendum and Kashmir 
through the Instrument of Accession (a legal document) 
executed by Maharaja Hari Singh (ruler of the Jammu & 
Kashmir) were included in the Indian Union. The Indian 
Constitution that came into force in 1950 went a step further, 
recognising four different categories of States and territories in 
the first Schedule. Part A was comprised of former British India 
provinces, which had a governor and a Legislature. Part B was 
comprised of former Princely States governed by a 'raj pramukh' 
while Part C was a combination of Princely States and chief 
commissioner's provinces governed by a chief commissioner. 
Part D was comprised of the lone territory of the Andaman and 
Nicobar Islands administered by the President through a Chief 
Commissioner/Other authority appointed by him. It was Part C 
states and part D territories that would go on to form the basis 
for the creation of Union Territories. *As per the Article 1(1)
of the Constitution, “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of 
States” rather than the Federation of States. *Article 2 provides 
for the admission or establishment of New States. *Article 3
provides for the power of the Parliament in the formation of 
New States and alteration of areas, boundaries and names of 
existing States. *Parliament can form new States through a 
simple majority. *Amendments made under Articles 2 and 3 
are out of the scope of Article 368. *Presently, India comprises 
28 States and 8 Union Territories. S.K. Dhar Commission 
1948 recommended the reorganization of States on the basis 
of administrative convenience instead of a linguistic basis. *In 
December 1948, the JVP committee was constituted by the 
Congress to scrutinize the recommendations of the S.K. Dhar 
Commission. *This committee included Jawahar Lal Nehru, 
Vallabh Bhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramaiya. *The committee, 
in its report presented in April 1949, officially rejected the 
demand for the reorganization of the States on linguistic basis. 
*Although the demise of Potti Sriramulu after the 56-day-long 
hunger strike forced the Indian Government for the formation of 
Andhra Pradesh on linguistic basis in October, 1953. *Andhra
Pradesh is the first State of India formed on the linguistic basis. 
*A States Reorganisation Commission under the Chairmanship 
of Fazal Ali was constituted for the formation of new States in 
1953. *Two other members of this Commission were – K.M. 
Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru. *Some of the recommendations of 
this commission were implemented in the States Reorganisation 
Act, 1956.

The Citizenship
*The Constitution deals with the citizenship from Articles 5 
to 11 under Part II. 
*India, like Britain, adopted the system of single citizenship. 
*Article 11 empowers the Parliament to make laws regarding 
citizenship. 
*The Indian Citizenship Act was passed by Parliament in 1955.
*It prescribes five ways of acquiring citizenship – (1) By Birth, 
(2) By Descent, (3) By Registration, (4) By Naturalisation 
and (5) By incorporation of territory. 
*The Indian Citizenship Act 1955, prescribes three ways of 
losing citizenship, whether acquired under the Act or prior 
to it under the Constitution – (1) By Renunciation, (2) By 
Termination and (3) By Deprivation. 
*Article 6 provides for the rights of citizenship of certain 
persons who have migrated to India from Pakistan. 
*Article 7 provides for the rights of citizenship of certain 
migrants to Pakistan. 
*Article 8 provides for the rights of citizenship of certain 
persons of Indian origin residing outside India. 
*Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State 
are not to be citizens as mentioned in Article 9. *As per the 
Section 5 (1) (a) of the Citizenship Act 1955, a person of Indian 
origin can acquire citizenship by registration if a person of 
Indian origin who has been a resident of India for 7 years before 
applying for registration. The Act has been amended : in 1957, 
1985, 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005 and 2015, 2019.
*Under section 7A of The Citizenship Act, 1955 (inserted by 
'The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2015) the Central government 
may, subject to such conditions, restrictions and manner as may 
be prescribed, on an application made on this behalf, register as 
an Overseas Citizen of India cardholder. Under this Amendment 
Act, it has been provided that no person, who or either of whose 
parents or grandparents or great grandparents is or has been a 
citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh or such other country as the 
central government may, by notification in the official Gazette, 
specify, shall be eligible for registration as an overseas citizen 
of India cardholder under this sub-section. 
* The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 was passed by the 
Parliament of India on 11 December, 2019. It amended the
Citizenship Act, 1955 by providing (section 6B) that illegal 
migrants of Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Parsi, Buddhist and Christian 
religious minorities who had come to India on or before 31 
December, 2014 due to religious persecution from Pakistan, 
Bangladesh and Afghanistan shall not be treated as illegal 
migrants for the purpose of this Act, and by enabling grant of 
citizenship via certificates of registration/naturalisation, but 
subject to conditions. (Muslims are not included in this Act). 
This Act came into force on 10 January, 2020. Citizenship 
(Amendment) Rules, 2024 have been notified on 11 March 2024, 
which are rules for implementing section 6B of the Citizenship 
Act, 1955. *This Act does not apply to the tribal areas of Assam, 
Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura, which are included in the Sixth 
Schedule of the Constitution. *This Act does not apply even 
in the areas coming to the inner line under the Bengal Eastern 
Frontier Regulation, 1873.

Fundamental Rights
*The first explicit Demand for the Fundamental Rights (FR) 
came in the form of the "Constitution of India Bill, 1895" 
which was inspired by Bal Gangadhar Tilak. The Motilal Nehru 
Report of 1928 demanded inalienable Fundamental Rights for 
the people of India. *The Congress adopted a resolution on 
Fundamental Rights at the Karachi Session of 1931, presided 
over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. *The Fundamental rights are 
enshrined in Part III of the Constitution from Articles 12 to 35. 
*Originally, the Constitution provided for seven fundamental 
rights – (1) Right to Equality, (2) Right to Freedom, (3) Right 
against Exploitation, (4) Right to Freedom of religion, (5) 
Cultural and Educational rights, (6) Right to Property and 
(7) Right to Constitutional remedies. *However, the Right to 
Property was deleted from the list of fundamental rights by the 
44th Amendment Act, 1978. *Now, the right to property is a 
legal right under Article 300-A in Part XII of the Constitution. 
Fundamental Rights are the guarantee against the arbitrary 
actions of the State. *The enforcement of fundamental rights 
(except the rights under Articles 20 and 21) can be suspended 
during the operation of a national emergency, by an order 
of the president. These rights are justiciable. *Fundamental 
Rights in the Indian Constitution are often compared with 
the Bill of Rights in the Constitution of the U.S.A. Part III 
of the Indian Constitution is rightly regarded as the Magna 
Carta of India. *The Fundamental Rights are defended and 
guaranteed by the Constitution. *Article 14 provides for 
Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. *The 
Right to equality is enshrined in the Constitution from Articles 
14 to 18. *Prohibition of discrimination only on grounds of 
religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15). *Article 
16- Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. 
*Article 17- Abolition of untouchability and prohibition of its 
practice. *Article 18 – Abolition of titles except military and

[[PDF_PAGE:106]]
academic. *The Right to freedom is described in Articles 19 
to 22. Article 19 guarantees all citizens six rights. *These are – 
Article 19(1) (a) – Right to freedom of speech and expression, 
Article 19 (1) (b) – Right to assemble peacefully and without 
arms, Article 19(1) (c) – Right to form associations or unions 
or cooperative societies, Article 19(1) (d) – Right to move 
freely throughout the territory of India, Article 19 (1)(e) – 
Right to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India and 
Article 19(1) (g) – Right to practice any profession or to carry 
on any occupation, trade and business. *Article 20 provides 
for protection in respect of conviction for offences. *Protection 
of life and personal liberty is described in Article 21. *Eighty 
– Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 made free 
and compulsory education (for all children of the age 6 to 14 
years) a fundamental right and added Article 21A. *Article 22 
provides for protection against arrest and detention in certain 
cases. Right against exploitation is described in Articles 23 
and 24. *Article 23 provides for the prohibition of traffic in 
human beings and forced labour. *Article 24 provides for the 
prohibition of employment of children (below the age of 14 
years) in factories, etc. *The Right to freedom of religion is 
described in Articles 25 to 28. *Articles 29 and 30 are related 
to the cultural and educational rights of minorities. *Article 32 
provides for Constitutional remedies. *Dr. Ambedkar called 
Article 32 as 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very 
heart of it/ "heart and soul". *The Supreme Court (under Article 
32) can issue writs only for the enforcement of fundamental 
rights, and the High Courts (under Article 226) can issue writs 
not only for the enforcement of fundamental rights but also 
for any other purpose. *Five kinds of writs are mentioned in 
Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution:
(1) Habeas Corpus (to have the body of ) – The writ of Habeas 
Corpus can be issued against both public authorities as well 
as private individuals who have detained another person to 
produce the body of the latter before it.* If the detention is 
found to be illegal, the detained person would be set free.* 
This writ is the bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary 
detention.
(2) Mandamus (We command) – It is a command issued 
by the court against a public official, any public body, a 
corporation, an inferior court, a tribunal or a government, 
asking them to perform official duties that one has failed 
or refused to perform.
(3) Prohibition (to forbid) – It is issued by a higher court 
to a lower court or tribunal to prevent the latter from 
exceeding its jurisdiction or usurping a jurisdiction that 
it does not possess.
(4) Certiorari (to be certified) – It is issued on the grounds 
of excess of jurisdiction or lack of jurisdiction or error 
of law. It is issued by a higher court to a lower court to 
transfer a case pending with the latter to itself or to quash 
the order of the latter in a case.
(5) Quo – Warranto (By what authority or warrant) – It 
is issued by the court to enquire into the legality of the 
claim of a person to a public office.
*Article 358 provides for the suspension of provisions of 
Article 19, during emergencies. *Article 359 provides for 
the suspension of the enforcement of fundamental rights 
except Articles 20 and 21 during emergencies (after the 44th
Constitutional Amendment Act). *The Supreme Court, in its 
judgment in the case of Bachan Singh Vs State of Punjab, held that 
the sentencing discretion inherent in section 302 of the 
IPC is not violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Indian 
Constitution.

Directive Principles of State Policy
*The Directive Principles of State Policy are mentioned in Part 
IV of the Indian Constitution from Articles 36 to 51. 
*The idea of Directive Principles of State Policy is borrowed 
from the Irish Constitution.
*Article 37 deals with the application of the principles contained 
in this part. 
*The Directive Principles are non – justiciable. *The 
Constitution (Article 37) itself says that these principles are 
fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the 
duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
*They embody the concept of a ‘Welfare State’. *Article 38 
says, the State is to secure a social order for the promotion of 
the welfare of the people. *Article 39A, added by the 42nd
Amendment, provides for the equal justice and free legal 
aid to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are 
not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other 
disabilities.
*Organisation of Village Panchayats (Article 40). *Right to 
work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases 
(Article 41). *According to the Article 42, the State shall make 
provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and 
for maternity relief. According to Article 43, the State shall 
endeavour to secure, for all workers, work and living wage, 
and to promote the cottage industry. *Participation of workers 
in the management of industries (Article 43 A). *Promotion 
of cooperative societies (Article 43 B). *Uniform Civil Code 
for the citizens (Article 44). *The State shall endeavour to 
provide early childhood care and education to children below 
the age of six years (Article 45). *Promotion of educational and 
economic interests of scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and 
other weaker sections (Article 46). *It is the duty of the State to 
raise the level of the nutrition and the Standard of living and to 
improve public health (Article 47). *Organisation of Agriculture 
and Animal Husbandry (Article 48). *Article 48A provides 
for the protection and improvement of the environment and 
safeguarding of forests and wild life. *Article 49 provides for 
the protection of monuments, and places and objects of national 
importance. *Separation of judiciary from executive (Article 
50). *Promotion of international peace and security (Article 51).

Fundamental Duties
*The Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution are inspired 
by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR. *These were added 
on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee 
through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. *This 
amendment added a new part (Part IV A) which consists of 
only one article, that is, Article 51 A. *Presently, the number 
of Fundamental Duties, as per the Article 51 A, is 11, whereas 
originally, at the time of its inclusion in the Constitution, the 
number was 10. The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by the 
86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. 
*According to Article 51 A, it shall be the duty of every citizen 
of India –
(a) To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and 
institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem;
(b) To cherish and follow the noble ideas which inspired our 
national struggle for freedom;
(c) To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity 
of India;
(d) To defend the Country and render national service when 
called upon to do so;
(e) To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood 
amongst all the people of India; to renounce practices 
derogatory to the dignity of women;
(f) To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite 
culture;
(g) To protect and improve the natural environment- including 
forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion 
for living creatures;
(h) To develop the scientific temper, humanism and spirit of 
inquiry and reform;
(i) To safeguard public property and to abjure violence;
(j) To Strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual 
and collective Activity.
(k) Who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for 
education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between 
the age of six and fourteen years (added by 86 Amendment 
Act, 2002).

The President
*The President of India is the head of the Indian State, the first 
citizen, and acts as the symbol of unity, integrity and solidarity 
of the nation. *According to Article 52, ‘There shall be a 
President of India’. *According to Article 53, the executive 
power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be 
exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate 
to him in accordance with this Constitution. *According to 
Article 54, the President shall be elected by the members of an 
electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses 
of Parliament and elected members of the Legislative Assembly 
of the States. *70th Amendment Act, 1992 (effective from 01-
06-1995) provided for the inclusion of the elected members 
h on TG-@freepdfhall

[[PDF_PAGE:157]]
of legislative assemblies of the National Capital Territory of 
Delhi and the Union territory of Puducherry in the electoral 
college for the election of the President. *Nominated members 
and members of Legislative Councils do not participate in 
the election of the President. *According to Article 55(3), the 
election is held in accordance with the system of proportional 
representation by means of the single transferable vote and 
the voting is done by secret ballot. *All doubts and disputes 
in connection with the election of the President are enquired 
into and decided by the Supreme Court, whose decision is 
final. *The Election of the President cannot be challenged on 
the grounds that the electoral college was incomplete. (due to 
any vacancy of members) *Article 58 describes the eligibility 
criteria (a citizen of India, has completed the age of 35 years 
and is qualified for election as a member of the House of 
the People, and is not ineligible due to holding any office 
of profit under Article 58(2)) for election as President. 
*Further, the nomination of a candidate for election to the 
office of President must be subscribed by at least 50 electors as 
proposers and 50 electors as seconders. *Every candidate has 
to make a security deposit of Rs. 15000. The security deposit is 
liable to be forfeited in case the candidates are not elected and 
the number of valid votes polled by such candidates does not 
exceed one-sixth of the number of votes necessary to secure the 
return of a candidate at such election. *The President's term of 
office is five years from the date on which he enters his office 
(Article 56). *According to Article 56 (1)(a), the President 
submits his resignation in writing under his hand addressed 
to the Vice- President of India. The Vice-President shall 
immediately inform, about the resignation, to the speaker of the 
Lok Sabha (Under Article 56(2)). *Further under Article 56(1)
(b) he can also be removed from the office by the process of 
Impeachment (mentioned under Article 61) *The Article 57 
defines the eligibility of re-election, to the post of the President, 
for a person. The only ground for impeachment specified in the 
Art. 61(1) is the violation of the Constitution. *No President 
has so far been impeached. *When a vacancy occurs in the 
office of the President due to his resignation, removal, death 
or otherwise, the Vice–President acts as the President until a 
new President is elected. *Further, when the sitting President 
is unable to discharge his functions due to absence, illness or 
any other cause, the Vice–President discharges his functions 
until the President resumes his office. *In case the office of 
the Vice–President is vacant, the Chief Justice of India (or if 
his office is also vacant, the senior-most judge of the Supreme 
Court available) acts as the President or discharges the functions
of the President. *According to Article 59(1), if any person 
who is a member of either House of Parliament or a House 
of the State legislature is elected as President, he is deemed 
to have vacated his seat in that house on the date on which he 
enters upon his office as President. *The oath of office to the 
President is administered by the Chief Justice of India (Art. 
60). *Currently, the salary of the President is 5 Lakh per month. 
It is paid from the Consolidated Fund of India. *According 
to Article 77, the conduct of businesses of the Government of 
India is formally done in the President's name. 
*He can summon a joint sitting of both the houses of 
Parliament (Art.108). *When a bill is sent to the President after 
it has been passed by the Parliament, he can give his assent to 
the bill or withhold his assent to the bill, or return the bill (if 
it is not a money bill) for reconsideration by the Parliament. 
However, if the bill is passed again by the Parliament, with or 
without amendments, the President has to give his assent to the 
bill. *A bill becomes an Act after the assent of the President. 
*The President cannot return a money bill for reconsideration. 
*Money bill is introduced in the Parliament, that too in Lok 
Sabha only with his prior recommendation. *He can promulgate 
ordinances when the Parliament is not in Session (Art.123). 
*These ordinances must be approved by the Parliament within six 
weeks from its reassembly. *He can also withdraw an ordinance at 
any time. *Article 72 of the Constitution empowers the President to 
grant pardons to persons and to suspend, remit, respite, reprieve or 
commute sentences in certain cases. *He has the power to consult 
the Supreme Court (Art. 143). *He can declare any area as a 
scheduled area and has powers with respect to the administration 
of scheduled areas and tribal areas. He is the supreme commander 
of defence forces (Army, Navy and Air-force) of India. *The 42nd
Amendment Act, 1976 made a provision that made the President 
bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the 
Prime Minister. *The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 (enacted by the 
Janta Party Government) authorized the President to require the 
Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice either generally or 
otherwise. However, he shall act in accordance with the advice 
tendered after such reconsideration.

The Council of Ministers
*The Central Council of Ministers includes Prime Minister, 
Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State and Minister of State 
(independent). *According to Article 74(1), there shall be a 
Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to 
aid and advise the President, who shall, in the exercise of his 
functions, act in accordance with such advice. However, the 
President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider 
such advice, and the President shall act in accordance with the 
advice tendered after such reconsideration (added through 
the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act 1978). *The advice 
tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired 
into in any court [Article 74 (2)]. *According to Article 75 
(1), the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President 
and other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the 
advice of the Prime Minister. *According to Article 75 (1A), 
the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, 
in the Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15% of the total 
strength of the Lok Sabha. This provision was added by the 91st
Amendment Act, 2003. *As per Article 75(2), the Ministers 
shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. *The 
Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the 
Lok Sabha. *The term ‘Cabinet’ was mentioned only in clause 
(3) of the Article 352 of the Constitution and it was inserted 
by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act. It did not find
a place in the original content of the Constitution. *Cabinet 
includes Cabinet Ministers and the Prime Minister. *Due to the 
Ministerial Responsibility, for every act of the bureaucrats, 
the concerned Minister is answerable to the Parliament. *The 
Central Cabinet Secretariat is directly under the control of Prime 
Minister. Its administrative head is the Cabinet Secretary, who 
is the ex-officio chairman of the Civil Services Board. *A 
person who is not a member of either house of the Parliament 
can also be appointed as a minister, but within six months, he 
must become a member (either by election or by nomination) 
of either house of the Parliament, otherwise he ceases to 
be a minister. *The President administers the oath of office 
and secrecy to the Prime Minister and other ministers. *The 
Prime Minister is the Chairman of Union Cabinet meetings. 
*According to Article 78, it shall be the duty of the Prime 
Minister to communicate to the President all decisions of the 
Council of Ministers and to furnish such information relating 
to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals 
for legislation as the President may call for. The Prime Minister 
submits his resignation to the President. The ministries of 
departments are created by the President on the advice of the 
Prime Minister under the Government of India (Allocation of 
Business) Rules 1961, which are rules made by the President 
under Article 77 of the Constitution. There are 53 ministries at 
present in the Government of India. *The number of Ministries 
at the centre on 15 August 1947 was 18.

The Attorney-General and 
the C.A.G.
*The Indian Constitution provides for the office of the Attorney 
General for India. *He is the highest law officer in the country. 
*The President shall appoint a person who is qualified to be

The Parliament (1)
*Parliament is the legislative organ of the Union Government. 
*Articles 79 to 122 in Part V of the Indian Constitution 
deal with the Parliament. *According to Article 79, the 
Parliament of India consists of the President and the two 
houses - House of the People and the Council of States. 
*Lok Sabha is also known as the "House of the People". 
*Its maximum strength is 550. At present, it has 543 
(States-524, UTs-19) members. *Out of 550 members, at 
most 530 members are representative of states, 20 members 
are representative of Union territories. If, in the opinion 
of the President, there is not enough representation of the 
Anglo-Indian Community in the Lok Sabha, then he could 
nominate two members of that community to the Lok Sabha. 
In this regard, the arrangements related to the Anglo-Indian 
Community have not been extended beyond the stipulated 
date (25 January, 2020) by 'The Constitution (One Hundred 
and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019' [The Constitution (One 
Hundred and Twenty-Sixth Amendment) Bill, 2019]. Thus, 
the arrangements for the nomination of two members of the 
Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha have ended. *The 
allocation of state-wise seats in the Lok Sabha is based on 
the Census of 1971. *According to the 84th Constitutional 
h on TG-@freepdfhall

[[PDF_PAGE:213]]
Amendment Act, 2001, the next assessment shall be held after 
the year 2026. *In Lok Sabha seats are allotted on the basis of 
the population. *The normal tenure of Lok Sabha is 5 years
from the date of its first meeting after the general elections but 
it can be dissolved by the President in between. *Under the 
Article 83(2) Proviso, Lok Sabha can be extended during 
the time of National Emergency for one year at a time. *In 
any case of extension, it can't continue beyond the period of 
6 months after the emergency has ceased to operate. *The 
qualifications of a person in order to be elected a member of 
Lok Sabha are (a) He must be a citizen of India and (b) He must 
not be less than 25 years. (c) He must make and subscribe to 
an oath (d) He must possess other qualifications prescribed by 
the Parliament by law.
*According to Article 93, the Speaker and the Deputy 
Speaker are elected by Lok Sabha from among its members. 
*Suspension of Lok Sabha (Adjournment/Adjournment Sine 
die of Lok Sabha sitting) is called up by the Speaker, whereas 
prorogation and dissolution of Loksabha is called up by the 
President of India. *According to Article 94 (b), the Speaker 
of Lok Sabha addresses his resignation in writing to the Deputy 
Speaker and vice-versa.
*The speaker of Lok Sabha is removed from his Post by a 
resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of Lok 
Sabha and such resolution shall not be moved until and unless a 
14-day advance notice is given. *While a resolution of removal 
of the Speaker or Deputy Speaker is under consideration, 
the Speaker/Deputy Speaker concerned can not preside but both 
have the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of the 
house. *While the proposal of removal of the Speaker or Deputy 
Speaker is in process, the Speaker or Deputy Speaker (as the 
case may be) have the right to vote in first instance but not in 
the case of equality of votes. *The Speaker of Lok Sabha uses 
his casting vote only in case of a tie. *Lok Sabha Secretariat 
directly functions under the Speaker of Lok Sabha. *After the 
general elections, the Protem Speaker administers the oath to 
the newly elected members of Lok Sabha. *As provided by 
the Constitution, the Speaker of the last Lok Sabha vacates 
his office immediately before the first meeting of the newly 
elected Lok Sabha. Therefore, the President appoints a senior 
member of the Lok Sabha as the Pro-tem Speaker. *Article 
85(1) empowers the President to summon each house of the 
Parliament if he thinks fit. *In any case, the interval between 
the two consecutive sessions of the houses cannot be more than 
six months. (*Thus as per the Constitution, it is mandatory 
for Lok Sabha to meet at least twice a year. *According to 
Article 100(3), the quorum of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
shall be 1/10th of the total members of the respective houses. 
*Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of Lok Sabha seats 
(80) followed by Maharashtra (48) and West Bengal (42). In 
January, 2022 the Election Commission of India (ECI) has 
increased the expenditure limits for candidates, contesting in 
the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly polls. The ECI hiked 
the poll expenditure limit upto Rs. 95 lakh from the existing 
Rs. 70 Lakhs for the Lok Sabha election. For the state assembly 
elections, the expenditure limit has been enhanced to Rs. 40 
lakh from Rs. 28 lakh. For small states, revised expenditure for 
the Loksabha is increased by Rs. 75 Lakhs from Rs. 54 Lakhs. 
While, in the case of small state assembly it is increased to 
Rs. 28 Lakhs from the previous limit of Rs. 20 Lakhs. *First 
Lok Sabha elections were held from 25 October, 1951 to 21 
February, 1952. *The elections were conducted for 489 seats. 
*First Meeting of Lok Sabha took place on 13th May, 1952. 
*Ganesh Vasudev Mavlankar became the first Speaker of 
the Lok Sabha and remained in this post till his death on 27 
February, 1956. M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar was the speaker 
for the remaining tenure of the first Lok Sabha. In 1954, the 
first resolution/motion for removal of the speaker was brought 
against the first Speaker of Lok Sabha, G.V. Mavlankar, by 
Vigneshwar Missir (Socialist Party M.P. from Bihar), J.B. 
Kriplani and some other members of Opposition in the Lok 
Sabha which was rejected by the Lok Sabha. *First Deputy 
Speaker of Lok Sabha was M.A. Ayyangar. *The First woman 
speaker of Lok Sabha was Meira Kumar. *The Speaker of the 
present (18th) Lok Sabha is Om Birla.

The Parliament (2)
*The Upper House of the Parliament is also known as the 
Rajya Sabha. It is also known as the 'Council of States'. 
*The Maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is fixed at 250. 
According to Article 80, the Rajya Sabha consists of not 
more than 238 members from the States and Union Territories 
(elected indirectly) and 12 other members are nominated by the 
President from amongst the persons having special knowledge 
or practical experience in the field of literature, science, art 
and social service (Present Strength is 245, out of which 12 
are nominated members). *Representatives of each state shall 
be elected by the elected members of the legislative assembly 
of the state in accordance with the system of proportional 
representation by means of the single transferable vote. *Only 3 
Union territories (Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir) 
out of 8 have representatives in Rajya Sabha. *Rajya Sabha is 
a Permanent house. Hence it is not subject to dissolution. *As 
nearly as possible 1/3rd members of the Rajya Sabha retire at 
the end of every second year. *The term of its members is 6 
years. *A Person to be elected as a member of Rajya Sabha 
must fulfil two criteria- (1) he must be a citizen of India and 
(2) he must not be less than 30 years of age. In addition to the 
prior two conditions, he must be an elector for a parliamentary 
constituency in India. *The Vice-President of India is the exofficio chairman of the Council of States/Upper House of 
Parliament. *When the Vice-President acts as the President 
he shall not be entitled to get the salary and allowances of the 
Chairman of Rajya Sabha. For this period, he receives salary 
and allowances of the President. *Rajya Sabha elects a deputy 
chairman from amongst its members. *The Deputy Chairman 
gives his resignation in writing to the Chairman. *Rajya Sabha 
has the power to remove the Deputy Chairman from his post, 
by a resolution passed by the absolute majority of the total 
members of Rajya Sabha. Such resolution can be moved only 
after giving at least 14 days' notice. *When the post of Chairman 
is vacant, the deputy chairman will perform the duties of the 
chairman. *While presiding over the Rajya Sabha, the Deputy 
Chairman can't vote in general, he can only exercise a casting 
vote in case of a tie. *When a resolution to remove the VicePresident from his office is under consideration, he will not be 
presiding as the Chairman and when a resolution of removal 
of the Deputy Chairman is under consideration, he will not be
presiding as the Deputy Chairman. *The representation of states 
in Rajya Sabha is given in proportion to their population. *For 
a quorum, there must be the presence of one-tenth of the total 
number of members in the Rajya Sabha. *The Representation 
of People Act 1951 (through an amendment in 2003) made 
a provision that any person can contest from anywhere for 
Rajya Sabha even if he is a resident of any other state. Now for 
contesting Rajya Sabha elections, a person must be an elector 
in a parliamentary constituency anywhere in India. *The 4th 
Schedule of the Indian Constitution enumerates the allocation 
of Rajya Sabha seats for states and union territories. *Article 
249 states that if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution with a 2/3 
majority of its members present and voting, the Parliament can 
make laws in the national interest regarding the subjects of the 
state list, which are specified in the resolution. *It is valid for a 
period of 1 year, but it can be extended by passing a resolution. 
*Article 250 empowers the Parliament to legislate with respect 
to any matter in the state list if the proclamation of emergency 
is in operation but, six months after the emergency ceases to 
operate, it automatically expires. *Article 252 empowers the 
Parliament to legislate for two or more states by consent and 
adoption of such legislation by any other state. *According to 
Article 253, Parliament has the power to make any law for 
the whole or part of the territory of India for implementing 
international agreements or conventions with any other country 
or any decision made at any international conference.

The Parliament (3)
Conduct of Business and 
Legislative Procedure
*The Parliament of India is the supreme legislative body. 
*India has a parliamentary system of Government based on 
the Westminster model. *The Right to amend the constitution 
is vested in the Parliament under Article 368. *Maximum 
time gap between the two sessions of parliament is 6 months. 
*Lok Sabha speaker, Deputy speaker, Secretary General, Rajya 
Sabha chairman, Deputy chairman etc. are called officials of 
parliament. *There are usually three sessions in a year, i.e. 
Budget session, Monsoon session and Winter session. *If 
any member of Parliament remains absent for 60 days from 
all meetings without informing to the respective house, then 
the House may declare his seat vacant. *Article 105 of the 
Indian Constitution lays down the privileges and immunities 
of the members of Parliament. *For making International 
treaties effective, the Parliament can make laws in the state list 
without the consent of the state. *Speaker or chairman of the 
House can prohibit any member and allow any other member 
to speak. This is called Yielding the floor. *When a member 
of parliament changes party allegiance, leaving one political 
party and joining another political party in the Parliament, it is 
called Crossing the floor. *Zero Hour is a unique feature of 
the Parliamentary system of India. It can be a maximum of one 
hour, which is around 12 noon to 1:00 pm in Lok Sabha (its 
duration is not fixed in the Rules). *A money bill can only be 
introduced in Lok Sabha and that too on the recommendation 
of the President of India. It cannot be introduced in Rajya 
Sabha. *Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend a money bill and 
must return it within 14 days, after which, Lok Sabha may 
accept or reject its recommendations. If the money bill is not 
returned within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses in 
the form passed by Lok Sabha. *According to Article 108, the 
President summons both the Houses for a joint sitting to resolve 
the deadlock between the two houses over the passage of a bill. 
*According to Article 118(4) the speaker shall preside over a 
joint sitting of two houses of parliament. *The Joint sitting of 
two Houses of Parliament is called up only for ordinary bills 
or non-money financial bills. The Joint sitting of two houses
of Parliament is not called for Money Bills and Constitution 
Amendment Bills. *Since 26 January, 1950 joint sitting of two 
Houses has been invoked only for three bills- the first one was 
in 1961 for the Dowry prohibition bill, second one was for 
the Banking service commission (repeal) Bill in 1978 and 
third one in 2002 for the prevention of terrorism Bill. *Any 
ordinary bill can be introduced in any house of parliament. *The 
Speaker has power to decide whether a bill is a money bill 
or not. *To withdraw the funds from the Consolidated Fund 
of India, the government needs to pass appropriation bills. 
*According to Article 116 of the Indian Constitution, when 
an appropriation bill is not passed and the government needs 
funds then Lok Sabha has the power to withdraw funds from 
the consolidated fund of India through a Vote on Account, for a 
fixed period of time. *The Estimates Committee is the largest 
among the Financial committes of Parliament. It consists 
of 30 members (all from the Lok Sabha). There is no Rajya 
Sabha member in the Estimates Committee. *The Secretariat 
of the Indian Parliament is free from the Government. *Indian 
Parliament established control over administration through 
parliamentary committees.

Parliamentary Committees 
*The Parliament is assisted by a number of Committees in 
the discharge of its duties. These committees are appointed 
or elected by Houses of the Parliament or nominated by the 
Speaker / Chairman. They perform their work under the 
direction of the Speaker / Chairman and submit their report 
to the House, or to the Speaker / Chairman as applicable. 
*Mainly the parliamentary committees are of two kinds – 
Standing committees and Ad-hoc committees. *The Standing 
committees are permanent (constituted every year or 
periodically) and work on a continuous basis while the Ad-hoc 
committees are temporary and cease to exist on completion of 
the task assigned to them. *Standing Committees are-
(i) Financial Committees
(ii) Department-related Standing Committees. (Total 24)
(iii) Committee of Enquiry
(iv) Committees to Scrutinise and Control 
(v) Committees relating to the day-to-day business of the 
House.
(vi) Housekeeping Committees or Service Committees.
*Financial committee includes the Public Accounts 
Committee, Estimates Committee and Public Undertakings 
Committee. *Most of the standing committees, leaving some 
committees, consist of members from Lok Sabha and Rajya 
sabha in the ratio of 2:1. *The Public Accounts committee 
consist of 22 members (15 from Lok sabha and 7 from Rajya 
Sabha). It examines various expenditure reports and accounts 
under the purview of the Parliament. *The Estimates 
Committee consists of 30 members elected every year by the 
Lok Sabha from among its members. All of its members are 
from Lok sabha. *Its function is to suggest alternative policies 
in order to bring about efficiency and economy in administration 
and to report improvements in organizations, efficiency or 
administrative reform, consistent with the policy underlying the 
estimates, may be effected.* Public Undertakings Committee
consists of 22 members (15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya 
Sabha). It analyses the accounts and workings of the state-owned 
PSU firms. It also checks the disinvestment policies of the various 
PSUs. Committee to Inquire includes the committee on petitions, 
the committee on privileges and the ethics committee. *The 
Petition committee in Lok Sabha consists of 15 members, while 
the petition committee in Rajya Sabha consists of 10 members. 
*Public Accounts Committee submits its report to the Lok Sabha 
Speaker. (Ordinarily Presents reports to the House; only when the 
House is not in session, it may present the report to the Speaker 
and later present it to the House). Generally, a member from the 
opposition in Lok Sabha is appointed as the chairperson of this 
committee by the speaker of Lok Sabha. There are a total of 24
Departmentally Standing Committees (DRSCs). Out of 24, 8 
under Rajya Sabha and 16 under Lok Sabha.

The Supreme Court
*An Integrated Judicial system has been established under the 
Indian Constitution in which the Supreme Court is at the top. 
*Below the Supreme Court there are various High Courts. 
*This single system of the Judiciary has been adopted from 
the Government of India Act 1935. *The Supreme Court of 
India was inaugurated on 28th January 1950. *Articles 124 to 
147 in Part V of the Indian Constitution deal with the Supreme 
Court. *The Supreme Court of India consists of the Chief 
Justice of the India and up to 33 other judges. *Earlier there 
were 30 Judges and a Chief Justice. Supreme Court (Number 
of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019 increased the number of 
Judges including Chief Justice from 31 to 34. The President 
of India appoints the judges of the Supreme Court. *The 
President appoints a Chief Justice after consultation with the 
other judges of the Supreme Court of India and the judges of 
the high courts. *The person to be appointed as a Judge of the 
Supreme Court must be a citizen of India and he should be, 
for at least 5 years, a Judge of a High Court or two or more 
such courts in succession; or he has been for at least ten years 
an advocate of a High Court or of two or more such courts in 
succession; or he must be a distinguished jurist in the opinion of 
President. *No minimum age is prescribed for the appointment 
of judges of the Supreme Court. *Parliament has the power to
increase the number of Judges in Supreme Court. *A person 
appointed as the Judge of the Supreme Court has to make and 
subscribe an oath or affirmation before the President. *Judges 
can give their resignation in writing to the President. *Judges 
of the Supreme Court can be removed by the President after the 
recommendation of the Parliament (address by each House). 
*Recommendation (Address) of Parliament for the removal of 
Judges must be passed by a special majority in each House of the 
Parliament. *The recommendation of Parliament is presented 
to the President in the same session. *The grounds on which 
removal of judges takes place are proved misbehaviour or 
incapacity. *These removals can be declared unconstitutional 
and illegal in the state of being extraordinary. *The Judges of 
the Supreme Court retire at the age of 65 years. *Salary and 
other allowances of the Supreme Court Judges are determined 
by Parliament. *Under Article 127, the Chief Justice of India 
can designate a judge of a High Court as an Ad hoc Judge of the 
Supreme Court for a temporary period to complete the quorum 
of the Judges in the Supreme Court (with the previous consent 
of the President and after consultation with the Chief Justice 
of High Court concerned). *The bench hearing a case related 
to the interpretation of the Constitution should have at least 5 
judges. *According to Article 129, the Supreme Court is a 
Court of Record. *It has the power to punish for its contempt. 
*Court of Record means a court whose proceedings are kept as a 
record and are available as an evidence of fact. Article 131 deals 
with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. Disputes 
between the Government of India and any of the States of the 
Union, the government of India and any State or States on one 
side and any other State or States on the other side or between 
two or more States comes under the original jurisdiction of 
the Supreme Court (only if the dispute involues a question 
on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends).

*According to the Constitution of India, the High Court 
occupies the top position in the judicial administration of the

1956, authorised the Parliament to establish a common High

Record. *Article 216 states that every High Court will consist

from time to time deem necessary to appoint. *A High Court is 
a Court of Record which means that the judgements proceedings 
and acts of the High Court are recorded for perpetual memory 
and testimony. *These records are admitted to be of evidentiary 
value and cannot be questioned when produced before any 
subordinate court. They are recognised as legal precedents 
and legal references and the court also has powers to punish 
for contempt of itself. *The judges of the High Courts are 
appointed by the President. *The President appoints them after 
consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the governor of the 
State, and (for Judges other than the Chief Justice) the Chief 
Justice of High Court concerned.
*A judge holds the office until he attains the age of 62 years. 
*He can resign from his office by writing to the President. *A 
judge can be removed from his office by the President on the 
recommendation of the Parliament. *The President can issue a 
removal order only after an address by the Parliament has been 
presented to him in the same session for such removal passed 
with a special majority (a majority of the total membership 
of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of 
the members present and voting in each House). *Just like a 
Supreme Court Judge, a High Court Judge can be removed from 
his office on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. 
*A person to be appointed as a judge of a High Court - should 
be a citizen of India, he should have held a judicial office in the 
territory of India for at least ten years or he should have been 
an advocate of a high court (or high courts in succession) for 
at least ten years. *According to Article 223, the President can
appoint a judge of a High Court as an acting chief justice of the 
High Court to perform the duties of the office of Chief Justice, 
when the office of the Chief Justice is vacant or the Chief Justice 
of the High Court is temporarily absent or the Chief Justice is 
unable to perform his duties of his office.
*Article 226 of the Constitution empowers the High Court to 
issue writs for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights of 
the persons or for any other purpose. Article 227 states that 
Every High Court shall have superintendence over all courts 
and tribunals (except relating to the Armed Forces) throughout 
the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.
*At present there are 25 High Courts and 7 of them have

Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are the Union Territories with 
their own High Court. Delhi has its own; Jammu and Kashmir

territories fall under the jurisdiction of different state High 
Courts. *The Parliament can extend the jurisdiction of a High 
Court. *The institution of the High Court originated in India 
in 1862. The High Courts were set up at Calcutta, Bombay and

of the High Court for the North-Western Provinces was shifted 
from Agra to Allahabad in 1869. *Article 233 (1) states that

state are made by the Governor of the state in consultation with 
the High Court. *Article 235 empowers the High Court to have 
control over all other subordinate courts in that state. *In India 
a person can be detained under Preventive Detention generally 
for a maximum period of 3 months, under certain conditions, 
it may exceed 3 months. *Lok Adalats (People’s Court) is 
one of the alternative dispute resolution mechanisms in India, 
it is a forum where cases pending or at a pre-litigation stage 
are settled. *A Lok Adalat can take up civil cases (including 
marriage & family) and compoundable criminal cases. *A Lok 
Adalat is usually presided over by a sitting or retired judicial

Emergency Provisions
*The Emergency provisions are contained in Part XVIII of 
the Constitution from Articles 352 to 360. These provisions 
enable the Central Government to meet any abnormal situations 
effectively.
*The Constitution stipulates three types of emergencies – 
(i) An emergency due to war, external aggression or armed 
rebellion (Art. -352).
(ii) An Emergency due to failure of Constitutional machinery 
in the state (Art. - 356).
(iii) Financial Emergency due to a threat to the financial 
stability or credit of India (Art. - 360).
*During an Emergency, the Central government becomes all 
powerful and the executive power of the Union extends to the 
giving of directions to any State as to the manner in which the 
executive power of the State is to be exercised. *Under Article 
352, the President can declare a national emergency when 
the security of India or a part of it is threatened by war or 
external aggression or armed rebellion. *The Proclamation of 
Emergency must be approved by both the Houses of Parliament 
by the special majority required by Article 352(6) within 
one month from the date of its issue. *If the proclamation of 
emergency is issued at a time when the Lok Sabha has been 
dissolved or the dissolution of the Lok Sabha takes place during 
the period of 1 month without approving the proclamation, then 
the proclamation survives for 30 days from the first sitting of 
the Lok Sabha after its reconstitution and ceases unless Lok 
Sabha also approves it within those 30 days, provided that the 
Rajya Sabha has in the meantime approved it. *If approved by 
both the Houses of Parliament the emergency continues for 
6 months from the date of passing of the Second approving 
resolution and may be extended for further six-month periods 
by resolutions of both Houses passed with the special majority 
under Article 352 (6).
*During a National Emergency, the Parliament becomes 
empowered to make laws on any subject mentioned in the State 
list. *The laws made by Parliament on State subjects become 
inoperative six months after the emergency has ceased to 
operate. The President can issue an ordinance on state subjects 
also, if the Parliament is not in session.

National Emergency is in operation, the President can modify
the Constitutional distribution of revenues between the Centre 
and the States. This modification operates only for a period 
not extending beyond the end of the financial year in which 
the proclamation ceases, and every such order must be laid 
before each House of Parliament. *According to Article 83 (2), 
while a proclamation of National Emergency is in place, the 
life of the Lok Sabha may be extended beyond its normal 
term (5 years) by a law of Parliament for one year at a time
(for any number of times). *However this extension cannot 
continue beyond a period of six months, after the emergency

*Articles 358 and 359 describe the effect of a National 
Emergency on Fundamental Rights. Article 358 deals with 
the suspension of enforcement of the Fundamental Rights 
guaranteed by Article 19 due to war or external aggression. No 
separate order for their suspension is required. *Article 359 
deals with the suspension of enforcement of other Fundamental 
Rights (Except those guaranteed by Articles 20 & 21). *Article 
359 authorises the President to suspend the right to move

house of the Parliament only by a simple majority. For any

within two months from the date of its issue. *Once approved
